source: Marqu - The Hebrew Gospel of Mark v1.2

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them: Some of you who are with{H5973} me shall not die{H4191} until{H5704} they see{H7200} [the light{H216}] of the kingdom{H4438} of God{H410}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses האור (ha'or, H216 — 'the light') — bracketed in the source, suggesting editorial restoration. Greek has ἐληλυθυῖαν ἐν δυνάμει ('come in power'). A back-translator from Greek would write בא בכח ('come in power'), NOT 'the light.' The Hebrew frames the kingdom as a visible light — connecting to Isaiah 60:1 ('arise, shine, for your light has come') and Psalm 36:10 ('in your light we see light'). This is a uniquely Hebrew theological concept.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the light of the kingdom of God.' Greek: 'the kingdom of God come in power.' Entirely different: luminous kingdom vs. powerful kingdom.
translation_notes: מקצת (miqtsat) — from קצה (qatseh, H7097 — 'end/extremity'), used in later Hebrew for 'a portion/some.' Standard OT usage is spatial ('end of'), but post-biblical usage shifted to quantitative ('some of').

verses.translation: After six{H8337} days{H3117} had passed{H5674}, he took{H3947} Keipha and Ya'aqov{H3290} and led{H5090} them upon one{H259} mountain{H2022}, very{H3966} high{H1364}; and they were all{H3605} alone{H905}. And there was a change{H8138} of the form{H6699} of his face{H6440}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שנוי צורת הפנים ('change of the form of the face') — a concrete, physical Hebrew description. Greek μετεμορφώθη ('was transfigured/metamorphosed') is a Greek philosophical term. A Hebrew author describes what was visibly observed — the face changed form. A back-translator from Greek would struggle to find an equivalent for μεταμόρφωσις and would likely transliterate or use השתנה ('changed'), not the elaborate construct שנוי צורת הפנים.

Uses נהגם (nahagam, H5090 — 'led them'), the verb for leading/driving flocks (Gen 31:18, Isa 11:6). Greek has ἀναφέρει ('carries up'). A back-translator from Greek would use העלה ('brought up'), not the shepherd-leading verb נהג.
greek_deviations: Hebrew mentions only Keipha and Ya'aqov. Greek adds καὶ τὸν Ἰωάννην ('and Yochanan'). This may reflect a shorter Hebrew Vorlage.
Hebrew: 'change of the form of the face.' Greek: 'was transfigured' (μετεμορφώθη). Different conceptual frames — visible observation vs. abstract transformation.

verses.translation: And his garments{H4403} were [ ] shining{H2094} and white{H3836} like snow{H7950}, such that no{H3808} man{H120} is able{H3201} to make{H6213} them so upon the face{H6440} of the ground{H127}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses על פני האדמה ('upon the face of the ground,' H127 — adamah). Greek has ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ('upon the earth'). The phrase פני האדמה is a specific Hebrew idiom appearing throughout the Torah (Gen 2:6, 4:14, 6:1, 7:3, 8:8). A back-translator from Greek would write על הארץ ('upon the earth'), not the idiomatic pnei ha'adamah.

Uses מזהירים (mazhirim, H2094 — 'shining/illuminating'), from the root זהר which carries dual meaning: 'to shine' AND 'to warn/enlighten' (Dan 12:3 — 'those who make wise shall shine'). Greek λευκά ('white') is purely visual. The Hebrew verb carries intellectual/spiritual connotation absent from Greek.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ὡς χιών ('as snow') and a comparison to a fuller's whitening: γναφεύς. Hebrew mentions snow but not the fuller/launderer.
translation_notes: The bracket [ ] in the source indicates a gap or lacuna in the Hebrew manuscript.

verses.translation: And Moshe{H4872} and Eliyahu{H452} appeared{H7200}, speaking{H1696} with Yeshua.

greek_deviations: Hebrew order: Moshe and Eliyahu. Greek order: Ἠλίας σὺν Μωϋσεῖ (Elijah with Moses). Hebrew preserves chronological priority (Torah before Prophets); Greek reverses it.

verses.translation: And Keipha answered{H6030} Yeshua and said{H559} to him: It is good{H2896} that we make{H6213} here{H6311} three{H7969} tents{H168} — for you one{H259}, and for Moshe{H4872} one, and for Eliyahu{H452} one.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אהלים (ohalim, H168 — 'tents'), the word for the Tabernacle dwelling-tents of Israel's wilderness period (Gen 12:8, 13:3; Ex 33:7ff). Greek σκηνάς ('booths') is the standard translation, but the Hebrew word naturally evokes the Sukkot festival and the wilderness Tabernacle tradition.

verses.translation: And he did not know{H3045} what{H4100} he was saying{H559}, for they were very{H3966} frightened{H6342}.
And a thick-cloud{H5645} formed, making{H6213} shadow{H6738} over them; and a voice{H6963} came{H935} from the cloud{H5645}: [saying] This is my son{H1121}, precious{H3368} — hear{H8085} him!

one_way_hebrew: Uses עב (av, H5645 — 'thick cloud/dark cloud'), NOT ענן (anan — 'cloud'). The av is the specific theophany cloud — the thick dark cloud at Sinai (Ex 19:9 — הנה אנכי בא אליך בעב הענן, 'behold I come to you in the thick cloud'; Deut 4:11, 5:22). Greek νεφέλη ('cloud') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would use ענן, not the Sinai-specific עב.

Uses צל (tsel, H6738 — 'shadow/shade'), connecting to Psalm 91:1 — 'in the shadow (צל) of the Almighty.' Greek ἐπισκιάζουσα ('overshadowing') is related but the Hebrew term evokes divine shelter and protection.

Uses יקר (yaqar, H3368 — 'precious/costly/rare') for the son, NOT אהוב (ahuv — 'beloved'). Greek has ἀγαπητός ('beloved'). A back-translator from Greek would use אהוב. The Hebrew says the son is 'precious/rare' (1 Sam 3:1 — the word of YHWH was yaqar). Different nuance: rarity and costliness vs. emotional affection.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'precious' (יקר). Greek: 'beloved' (ἀγαπητός). Different attributes of the son.
Hebrew: cloud 'making shadow.' Greek: cloud 'overshadowing.' The Hebrew is more concrete.
translation_notes: [שאמרת] is bracketed in the source, indicating editorial restoration.
textual_notes: The thick cloud (עב) with a voice speaking from it directly parallels the Sinai theophany (Ex 19:9, 24:15-18). The Transfiguration is portrayed as a second Sinai.

verses.translation: And immediately they looked{H5027} around{H5439} them and saw{H7200} nothing except{H905} Yeshua alone.

And as they descended{H3381} from the mountain{H2022}, Yeshua commanded{H6680} that they should not tell{H559} any man{H120} this vision{H4758} until{H5704} he returns{H7725} alive{H2416} from death{H4194}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses המראה (hamar'eh, H4758 — 'the vision/appearance'), the specific prophetic vision word used for Ezekiel's visions (Ezek 1:1, 8:3, 40:2) and Daniel's (Dan 10:7-8). Greek simply says μηδενὶ ἃ εἶδον διηγήσωνται ('should tell no one what they saw'). The Hebrew frames the Transfiguration as a מראה — a prophetic vision of the same class as Ezekiel's.

Uses יחזור חי ממות ('returns alive from death') — concrete Hebrew. Greek has ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῇ ('rise from the dead'). The Hebrew describes a journey: he goes to death and returns alive from it. A back-translator from Greek would write יקום מן המתים ('rise from the dead'), not 'return alive from death.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'this vision.' Greek: 'what they saw.' Hebrew uses a technical prophetic term; Greek is descriptive.
Hebrew: 'returns alive from death.' Greek: 'rise from the dead.' Different conceptual frame — return from a place vs. standing up from a state.

verses.translation: And they concealed{H5956} the matter among{H996} themselves.

greek_deviations: Greek has τὸν λόγον ἐκράτησαν ('they kept the word') — merely holding/retaining. Hebrew העלימוהו ('they concealed it') implies active hiding, from עלם (alam, H5956 — 'to hide/conceal'). Different implication: active concealment vs. passive retention.

verses.translation: And they asked{H7592} him: What does it mean that the Perushim say — and the scribes{H5608} after them — that Eliyahu{H452} must come{H935} first{H7223}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses הפרושים (haPerushim — 'the Perushim'), the native Hebrew name from פרש (parash, H6567 — 'to separate/distinguish'). Greek γραμματεῖς ('scribes') is a functional title. A back-translator from Greek would NOT produce the internal Hebrew party name with its etymological transparency.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'and the scribes after them' — implying the scribes follow the Pharisees' teaching. Greek has only γραμματεῖς ('the scribes').
translation_notes: חוייב — a Hebrew legal term meaning 'obligated/required.' No standard Strong's number; a later Hebrew development from the root חוב.
textual_notes: References Malachi 4:5 (Hebrew 3:23) — 'Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of YHWH comes.'

verses.translation: And he answered{H6030} and said{H559}: When Eliyahu{H452} comes{H935} first{H8462}, he shall restore{H5337} all{H3605} the world{H5769}. As it is written{H3789} that the Son{H1121} of God{H430} shall suffer{H5375} oppression{H5065} unto a shameful death{H4194}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בן האלוה (ben ha'Eloha — 'Son of God'). Greek has ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('Son of Man'). The Hebrew consistently uses 'Son of God' where the Greek has 'Son of Man.' If this Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, the translator would faithfully render 'Son of Man' as בן אדם. The use of 'Son of God' points to an independent Hebrew tradition.

Uses נגישה (negishah — 'oppression/exaction'), from נגש (nagash, H5065). This is the word for the Egyptian taskmasters who oppressed Israel (Ex 3:7, 5:6,10,13,14). The Son of God's suffering is described with Exodus-slavery vocabulary. Greek has πάθῃ ('suffer') and ἐξουδενωθῇ ('be treated with contempt') — generic terms. A back-translator would NEVER reach for the Egyptian-oppression verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Son of God' (בן האלוה). Greek: 'Son of Man' (υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου). Major christological difference.
Hebrew: 'suffer oppression unto a shameful death.' Greek: 'suffer many things and be set at nought.' Different descriptions of the suffering.
translation_notes: מגונה ('shameful/disgraceful') — a later Hebrew moral term. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: The phrase 'as it is written' points to Isaiah 53 — the Suffering Servant who bears oppression.

verses.translation: Indeed{H403} I say{H559} to you that Eliyahu{H452} came{H935} to them and they did{H6213} their desire{H7522} to him, as the writing{H3791} says{H559} of him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הכתיבה (hak'tivah — 'the writing'), a characteristically Hebrew way of referring to Scripture. This later Hebrew noun form from כתב (katav, H3789) is a native linguistic development. Greek γέγραπται ('it is written') is the standard form.

verses.translation: And when he came{H935} to the disciples, he found{H4672} a great{H7227} multitude{H5971} among{H996} them, and many{H7227} learned scholars debating{H3198} with them.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חכמים ומאותתים ('wise ones and lettered ones') — a Hebrew social description of the scribal class. Greek has γραμματεῖς ('scribes'). The Hebrew uses native categories: חכמים (learned/wise) and מאותתים (from אות — 'letter/sign,' meaning 'lettered/literate'). A back-translator from Greek would use סופרים (sofrim), not this descriptive Hebrew phrase.
translation_notes: מאותתים — from אות (ot — 'sign/letter'). Meaning 'lettered ones/scholars.' No standard Strong's number.

verses.translation: And when the people{H5971} saw{H7200} Yeshua coming{H935}, they were astonished{H8539} and went out{H3318} to meet him on the way{H1870}, and greeted him.
And he asked{H7592} them: What are you disputing{H2505} among{H996} yourselves?
And one{H259} man{H376} from the people{H5971} answered{H6030} and said{H559}: Rabbi, I have brought{H5090} my son{H1121} to you, for in his heart{H3820} is a satan{H7854}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שטן (satan, H7854 — 'adversary/accuser') — the Hebrew concept. Greek has πνεῦμα ἄλαλον ('mute spirit'). The Hebrew uses the uniquely Hebraic concept of a satan; the Greek uses the Hellenistic concept of a spirit (πνεῦμα). A back-translator from Greek would write רוח אלם ('mute spirit'), not שטן.
Locates the satan שבלבו ('in his heart') — the affliction is in the heart, a Hebrew anthropological concept. Greek mentions no location of the spirit within the body.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a satan in his heart.' Greek: 'a mute spirit.' Different entity and different location.

verses.translation: And in every{H3605} place{H4725} where it seizes{H3947} him, it casts him down{H5307} and compels{H3905} him to bring forth foam from his mouth{H6310}, and he gnashes{H5367} his teeth{H8127}. And I sought{H1245} from your disciples that they heal{H7495} him, and they were not able{H3201}.
And Yeshua said{H559}: O refusing{H3985} family{H4940}! How long shall I be{H1961} with{H5973} you? I will not bear{H5375} you! Bring{H5090} the man{H376}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses משפחה ממאנת ('refusing family'), from מאן (ma'an, H3985 — 'to refuse/be unwilling'). Greek has γενεὰ ἄπιστος ('faithless generation'). Hebrew ממאנת means active rebellion/refusal; Greek ἄπιστος means absence of faith. A back-translator would use חסרי אמונה ('lacking faith'), not the active-refusal verb מאן.
Uses משפחה (mishpachah, H4940 — 'family/clan') instead of דור (dor — 'generation'). Greek γενεά = 'generation.' The Hebrew addresses them as clan members — more intimate and more damning.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'refusing family.' Greek: 'faithless generation.' Different qualifier and different social unit.

verses.translation: And they brought{H5375} him before{H6440} him, and when he saw{H7200} him, immediately it tormented{H6087} him and threw him down{H5307} before{H6440} him, and he was rolling about and foaming.
And Yeshua asked{H7592} the father{H1}: How long has this been with him? And he said{H559}: From his youth{H5271} until{H5704} now{H6258}.

And continually{H8548} it throws{H7993} him into fire{H784} and into water{H4325} to kill{H4191} him. But if{H518} you are able{H3201} to do{H6213} anything, help{H5826} me with your lovingkindness{H2617}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בחסדך (b'chasdekha — 'with your lovingkindness/covenant-mercy,' H2617). Greek has σπλαγχνισθεὶς ἐφ' ἡμᾶς ('having compassion on us'). Hebrew חסד (chesed) is the untranslatable covenant-love word — God's steadfast loyal devotion. The father appeals to Yeshua's chesed, a concept far deeper than Greek σπλαγχνίζομαι ('compassion'). A back-translator from Greek would use רחם (racham — 'have compassion'), not the covenant-specific chesed.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'help me with your lovingkindness.' Greek: 'have compassion on us, help us.' Different appeal: covenant loyalty vs. emotional compassion.

verses.translation: And Yeshua said{H559} to him: If{H518} you are able{H3201} to believe{H539}, you will attain{H5381} all{H3605} things{H1697}.
And immediately the father{H1} of the son{H1121} cried out{H2199}, weeping{H1058}: I believe{H539}! Indeed{H403}, may it please{H3190} you to help{H5826} my faith{H530}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'may it please you to help my faith.' Greek: 'help my unbelief' (βοήθει μου τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ). Hebrew frames positively — strengthen my faith. Greek frames negatively — fix my unbelief.

verses.translation: And when he saw{H7200} that the people{H5971} were gathering{H622}, he commanded{H6680} the satan{H7854} [ ] to go out{H3318}, saying{H559}: Mighty{H2389} and mute{H483} satan{H7854}, I command{H6680} you to go out{H3318} from him, and after you shall not return{H7725} to him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שטן חזק ואלם ('mighty and mute satan'). Greek has τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἄλαλον καὶ κωφόν ('the mute and deaf spirit'). Hebrew uses חזק (chazaq, H2389 — 'strong/mighty') where Greek has κωφόν ('deaf'). Different attribute: 'mighty' vs. 'deaf.' Also, Hebrew addresses a 'satan'; Greek addresses a 'spirit' (πνεῦμα).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'mighty and mute satan.' Greek: 'mute and deaf spirit.' Different entity name and different attributes.

verses.translation: And it went out{H3318} screaming{H2199} and tormenting{H6087} him, and the lad{H5288} remained{H7604} as dead{H4191}, until{H5704} many{H7227} said{H559} he was dead{H4191}.
And Yeshua took{H3947} him by the hand{H3027}, and he returned{H7725} alive{H2416}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'he returned alive' (חזר חי). Greek: 'he arose' (ἀνέστη). Hebrew uses the same 'returned alive' phrase used for resurrection predictions — creating a micro-resurrection pattern.

verses.translation: And when they entered{H935} the house{H1004}, his disciples asked{H7592} him in secret counsel{H5475}: Why were we not able{H3201} to heal{H7495} him?

one_way_hebrew: Uses בסוד (b'sod, H5475 — 'in secret counsel/intimate council'). This is the Hebrew word for divine/prophetic council (Ps 25:14 — 'the sod of YHWH is for those who fear him'; Amos 3:7; Jer 23:18,22). Greek has κατ' ἰδίαν ('privately'). A back-translator would use בפרט ('privately'), not the theologically loaded סוד.

verses.translation: And he said{H559}: This measure{H4060} of satan{H7854} cannot be healed{H7495} except{H7535} by prayer{H8605} and fasting{H6685}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מדת השטן ('this measure of satan'), from מדה (middah, H4060 — 'measure/dimension/standard'). Greek has τοῦτο τὸ γένος ('this kind/race'). Hebrew מדה implies graded classification — satans have different 'measures' or grades. A back-translator from Greek would write מין ('type/kind'), not the measurement/standard term מדה.

verses.translation: [And they traveled{H5265}] from there and passed{H5674} through the Galil{H1551}, and he did not want{H7521} any man{H120} to know{H3045} it.

translation_notes: [ונסעו] is bracketed in the source, suggesting editorial restoration.

verses.translation: And he taught{H3925} his disciples and said{H559} to them: The Son{H1121} of God{H430} shall be betrayed{H898} and delivered{H4560} into the hand{H3027} of the wicked{H7451}, and they shall kill{H4191} him, and he shall return{H7725} alive{H2416} on the third{H7992} day{H3117}.

one_way_hebrew: Again בן האלוה ('Son of God') where Greek has υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('Son of Man'). Consistent Hebrew pattern.

Uses נבגד ונמסר ('betrayed and delivered') — TWO distinct verbs. בגד (bagad, H898) means 'to act treacherously' (used of covenant-breaking in Jer 3:20, 5:11, Mal 2:10-16). מסר (masar, H4560) means 'to hand over/deliver.' Greek has only παραδίδοται ('is delivered') — one verb. The Hebrew separates treachery from the physical handover.
Uses ביד הרעים ('into the hand of the wicked') — Greek has εἰς χεῖρας ἀνθρώπων ('into the hands of men'). Hebrew specifies the moral character (wicked); Greek is neutral (men).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Son of God.' Greek: 'Son of Man.'
Hebrew: 'betrayed and delivered.' Greek: only 'delivered.'
Hebrew: 'the wicked.' Greek: 'men.'
Hebrew: 'return alive on the third day.' Greek: 'after three days rise again.' Different timing and different verb.

verses.translation: And they did not understand{H995} the matter{H1697}, and they began{H2490} to question{H7592} him.

greek_deviations: Greek adds ἐφοβοῦντο αὐτὸν ἐπερωτῆσαι ('they were afraid to ask him'). Hebrew says they 'began to question him' — no fear mentioned.

verses.translation: And they came{H935} to Kfar Nachum{H3723}, and when they were in the house{H1004}, Yeshua asked{H7592} them: What were you disputing{H2505} on the way{H1870}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses כפר נחום (Kfar Nachum — 'Village of Comfort'), preserving the full semantic meaning of the Hebrew place name. Greek Καφαρναούμ (Capernaum) is a transliteration that obscures the meaning.

verses.translation: And they were silent{H8367}, for they had been disputing{H2505} which of them would be greatest{H1419}.
And Yeshua called{H7121} the twelve{H8147}{H6240} disciples and said{H559} to them: He [who desires{H7521}] to be great{H1419} [ ] among us shall be a servant{H8334} of all{H3605}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בינותינו ('among US') — first person plural, including himself in the group. Greek has πάντων ἔσχατος ('last of all'). The Hebrew includes Yeshua among those he addresses; the Greek has a different structure (last of all and servant of all).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall be a servant of all.' Greek: 'shall be last of all and servant of all.' Hebrew omits the 'last' concept.
translation_notes: Bracketed [שירצה] and [ ] in the source indicate editorial restorations.

verses.translation: And he took{H3947} one{H259} child{H5288} and placed{H7760} him in their midst{H8432}, and embraced{H2263} him, and said{H559}:
Whoever receives{H6901} [one{H259}] of these children{H5288} in my name{H8034} [receives{H6901}] me; and whoever receives{H6901} me does not receive me, but receives the one who sent{H7971} me.

translation_notes: Bracketed [אחד] and [יקבל] in the source indicate editorial restorations.

verses.translation: And Yochanan{H3110} answered{H6030} and said{H559}: We saw{H7200} a certain man{H120} who was healing{H7495} the satan-afflicted in your name{H8034}, and he is not of our fellowship{H2267}; and because of this we forbade{H4513} him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses המשוטנים ('the satan-afflicted') — a Hebrew verbal form meaning 'those under the influence of satan,' from שטן. Greek has ἐκβάλλοντα δαιμόνια ('casting out demons'). The Hebrew does not separate the 'casting out' action — instead it describes the people as afflicted and the man as 'healing' them. Different conceptual frame: Hebrew sees illness under a satan; Greek sees separate demons being expelled.

Uses מחבורתינו (mechaburatenu — 'of our fellowship'), from חבורה (chavurah, H2267). This is a specific Hebrew term for an intimate study/fellowship group — a distinctly Jewish social structure. Greek has οὐκ ἀκολουθεῖ ἡμῖν ('does not follow us'). Different concept: belonging to a fellowship vs. following a person.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'healing the satan-afflicted.' Greek: 'casting out demons.' Different action and different affliction.
Hebrew: 'not of our fellowship.' Greek: 'does not follow us.'

verses.translation: And Yeshua said{H559} to them: Do not forbid{H4513} him, for every{H3605} man{H120} who does{H6213} wonders{H6381} in my name{H8034} does not speak{H559} evil{H7451}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נפלאות (nifla'ot, H6381 — 'wonders'), the OT word for God's miraculous acts (Ex 3:20, 15:11, Ps 77:12, 78:12). Greek has δύναμιν ('power/mighty work'). A back-translator from Greek would use גבורה ('power'), not the Exodus-vocabulary nifla'ot.

verses.translation: And whoever is not against{H5048} us is with{H5973} us.
Every{H3605} man{H120} who gives{H5414} you one{H259} cup{H3563} in my name{H8034}, because you are anointed-ones{H4899} — truly{H571} I say{H559} to you, the reward{H1576} shall not be lost{H6}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses משיחים (meshichim — 'anointed ones,' H4899, plural of mashiach). Greek has ὅτι Χριστοῦ ἐστε ('because you are of Christ'). The Hebrew says the disciples ARE meshichim — anointed ones (plural, predicative). The Greek says they BELONG TO the Christ (singular, possessive). A back-translator from Greek would write של המשיח ('of the Messiah' — singular possessive), not 'you are meshichim' (anointed ones — plural). This reflects a Hebrew understanding where Messiah's followers share in his anointing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'you are anointed-ones' (plural identity). Greek: 'you are of Christ' (singular belonging). Fundamentally different: shared anointing vs. possessive relationship.

verses.translation: And whoever causes to stumble{H3782} one{H259} of the little ones{H6996} who believe{H539} in me — it would be more fitting{H7737} for him that they cast{H7993} him into the sea{H3220} with a millstone upon his neck{H6677}.

If{H518} your hand{H3027} causes stumbling{H3782}, cut it off{H3772}; for it is more fitting{H7737} for you to enter{H935} the Garden{H1588} of Eden{H5731} with one{H259} hand{H3027} than the fire of Gei-Hinnom{H1516} with two{H8147}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — GARDEN OF EDEN: Uses גן עדן (Gan Eden — 'Garden of Eden,' H1588 + H5731) where Greek has ζωήν ('life'). The Hebrew says 'enter the Garden of Eden' — the paradise of Genesis 2-3. Greek merely says 'enter into life.' A back-translator from Greek would write חיים (chayyim — 'life'), NEVER 'Garden of Eden.' The Hebrew preserves the native Jewish eschatological destination: return to the Garden of Eden. This is among the strongest one-way markers in the entire Gospel.

CRITICAL — GEI-HINNOM: Uses גיהנם (Gei-Hinnom — the Valley of Hinnom, H1516 + H2011). While Greek γέεννα is a transliteration of this, the crucial point is the PAIRING: Garden of Eden vs. Gei-Hinnom. In Hebrew, the eschatological contrast is native — Eden (paradise) vs. the valley where children were burned to Molech (2 Kings 23:10, Jer 7:31-32, 19:6). In Greek, the pair is 'life' vs. 'Gehenna' — which loses the Edenic contrast entirely.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Garden of Eden.' Greek: 'life' (ζωήν). Entirely different destination concept.
Greek adds εἰς τὸ πῦρ τὸ ἄσβεστον ('into the unquenchable fire'). Hebrew has 'fire of Gei-Hinnom.'
translation_notes: The Garden of Eden / Gei-Hinnom contrast creates a Genesis-framed eschatology: humanity's choice is between returning to Eden or descending to the valley of burning.
textual_notes: Gei-Hinnom (the Valley of Hinnom) — south of Jerusalem, where Molech worship with child sacrifice occurred (2 Kings 23:10, Jer 7:31-32, 19:2-6, 32:35). It became the symbol of divine judgment in Jewish eschatology.

verses.translation: To the place{H4725} where the venomous-things do not die{H4191}, and the fire{H784} does not rest{H5117}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — VENOMOUS THINGS: Uses הארסים (ha'arsim — 'the venomous things,' from ארס, eres — 'venom/poison'). Greek has ὁ σκώληξ αὐτῶν ('their worm'). The Hebrew does NOT say 'worm' — it says 'venomous things,' connecting to Numbers 21:6 where YHWH sent נחשים שרפים ('fiery/venomous serpents'). A back-translator from Greek 'worm' (σκώληξ) would use תולעת (tola'at — 'worm'), NEVER ארסים. The venomous things in Gei-Hinnom are serpent-like creatures of judgment — not common worms.

Uses אינו נח (eino nach — 'does not rest'), from נוח (nuach, H5117 — 'to rest'). This is the Sabbath-rest verb — the root of Noah's name. Greek has οὐ σβέννυται ('is not quenched'). The fire is described as anti-rest, anti-Sabbath — it finds no nuach. A back-translator from Greek would use לא תכבה ('is not extinguished'), not the theologically loaded 'does not rest.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'venomous things' (ארסים). Greek: 'worm' (σκώληξ). Entirely different creature.
Hebrew: 'the fire does not rest.' Greek: 'the fire is not quenched.' Different attribute: restlessness vs. unquenchability.
translation_notes: Both the 'venomous things' and the 'restless fire' quote Isaiah 66:24 — 'their worm (תולעתם) shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched.' But the Hebrew here uses ארסים instead of Isaiah's תולעת, suggesting an independent interpretive tradition about the nature of these creatures.
textual_notes: Isaiah 66:24 is the source text. The Hebrew Gospels' use of ארסים instead of תולעת shows the Hebrew author is interpreting, not merely quoting — identifying Isaiah's 'worms' as venomous/serpentine creatures.

verses.translation: And if{H518} your foot{H7272} causes stumbling{H3782}, cut it off{H3772}; for it is more fitting{H7737} for you to enter{H935} the Garden{H1588} of Eden{H5731} with one than to enter with two{H8147} into Gei-Hinnom{H1516}.
To the place{H4725} where the venomous-things do not die{H4191}, and the fire{H784} does not rest{H5117} and does not cease{H6461}.

And if{H518} your eye{H5869} causes stumbling{H3782}, pluck it out{H6131}; for it is more fitting{H7737} for you [ ] to enter{H935} into the Garden{H1588} of Eden{H5731} with one{H259} eye{H5869} than with two{H8147} into Gei-Hinnom{H1516}.
The place{H4725} where the venomous-things do not die{H4191}, and the fire{H784} is not extinguished{H3518}.

translation_notes: In this final repetition, the Hebrew uses נכבית (nikhbet — 'is extinguished,' H3518, from כבה) rather than the earlier נח ('rests'). The fire has two attributes across the three repetitions: it does not rest (v44,46) and it is not extinguished (v48).

verses.translation: Every{H3605} man{H120} by fire{H784} shall be refined, and every sacrifice shall be refined.

greek_deviations: Greek: πᾶς γὰρ πυρὶ ἁλισθήσεται ('everyone shall be salted with fire'). Hebrew uses יתעלם — possibly from עלם ('hidden/concealed') or a corrupted form. The meanings diverge significantly. The Greek connects directly to the salt discussion in v50; the Hebrew is more obscure.
translation_notes: This verse is textually difficult. The verb יתעלם may be from עלם (alam — 'to conceal/hide') or could be a corruption. The second clause 'כל אדם מרוצח' could mean 'every slain offering' (from רצח). The verse seems to describe a refining/purifying process by fire.

verses.translation: Good{H2896} is salt{H4417}, but if{H518} the salt{H4417} ceases{H6461}, with what shall we season{H1310}? Let there be salt{H4417} among you, and let there be peace{H7965} among you.

one_way_hebrew: Pairs מלח (melach — 'salt') and שלום (shalom — 'peace'). In Hebrew, the 'salt covenant' (ברית מלח, Num 18:19, 2 Chr 13:5) is a covenant of perpetual peace/preservation. The closing 'let there be salt among you and peace among you' ties salt to covenant-peace — a Hebrew theology of salt invisible in Greek.

Uses נבשל (nevasherl, H1310 — 'shall we cook/season'), from בשל (bashal — 'to cook/boil'). Greek ἀρτύσετε ('will you season') is about general seasoning. The Hebrew word specifically refers to cooking — salt as a cooking ingredient for the Temple offerings (Lev 2:13 — 'with all your offerings you shall offer salt').
textual_notes: Leviticus 2:13 — 'You shall season with salt every offering of your grain offering; you shall not allow the salt of the covenant of your God to be absent from your grain offering.' The command links salt, covenant, and offerings.

chapter_notes.summary: Mark 9 in Hebrew contains multiple critical one-way translation markers. The most striking are: (1) גן עדן ('Garden of Eden') vs. Greek 'life' — the Hebrew preserves the native Jewish eschatological destination (vv43,45,47); (2) ארסים ('venomous things') vs. Greek 'worm' — identifying Isaiah 66:24's creatures as serpentine rather than vermicular (vv44,46,48); (3) בן האלוה ('Son of God') where Greek has 'Son of Man' (vv12,31); (4) עב ('thick cloud') — the Sinai theophany term (v7); (5) יקר ('precious') vs. Greek 'beloved' for the divine son (v7); (6) משיחים ('anointed ones,' plural) vs. 'of Christ' (v41); (7) גיהנם paired with Garden of Eden creates a native Hebrew eschatological contrast absent from Greek. The chapter also shows consistent use of מראה (prophetic vision), סוד (secret counsel), מדה (measure/grade) for spiritual hierarchy, and חסד (covenant-love) — all Hebrew theological terms with no Greek equivalents.
